myth: Most English speakers live in Britain and the USA.
Most people who speak English learned it as a second language, in countries such as India, Nigeria, the Philippines, Pakistan and Germany. Native speakers are now a minority of all English speakers.

sec.t:
In the 400s and 500s CE, groups called the Angles, Saxons and Jutes sailed from what is now Germany and Denmark to Britain. Their speech became Old English, the language of the poem *Beowulf*. You would find it almost impossible to read today.

Then came the [[@vikings|Vikings]], who left everyday words such as *sky*, *egg* and *knife*. In 1066, William of Normandy conquered England, and for about 300 years its rulers spoke French. That's why English has pairs like *cow*, the farmer's word, and *beef*, the French-speaking diner's word, or *pig* and *pork*. By the time of [[@shakespeare|Shakespeare]], around 1600, English looked much more like it does now.

English never stays still when it moves. In India it gained words like *prepone*, the opposite of postpone, and *co-brother*, for the husband of your wife's sister. Indian English speakers say "do the needful" and "what is your good name?", phrases that sound odd in London but are perfectly clear in Lucknow.

American English changed too. Noah Webster's [[@dictionaries|dictionary]] of 1828 dropped the u from *colour* and *honour*. Nigerian, Singaporean, Australian and Caribbean English each have their own words and [[rhythm|rhythms]]. Many linguists now talk about "Englishes", in the plural, rather than one correct English.

Since the middle of the 1900s, English has become the main shared language for science, business and travel. Pilots and air traffic controllers on international flights must be able to use English, so a [[@airplanes-fly|plane]] from Delhi can land safely in Tokyo or New York. Most scientific papers today are published in English.

[[@internet-how|The internet]] pushed it further. Much of the early internet was built in the USA, and English is still the most common language on websites. This brings opportunities, but also worries. Some people fear that smaller languages lose speakers when young people switch to English. Others point out that most English learners keep their home language too and simply add another, the way millions of Indian children grow up speaking two or three.

text: Breakfast is wildly different around the world. In much of the United States, children pour a bowl of cereal or eat pancakes. In Japan it might be rice and soup. In south India, it's idli with sambar, and in Punjab a buttery aloo paratha. In Mexico, it could be crisp tortilla pieces in salsa.

What people eat depends on what grows nearby, how much time families have and old habits passed down for generations. Many breakfasts that seem unusual to outsiders are as normal to the people who eat them as toast is to others.

sec.t:
India alone has dozens of breakfasts. In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, children eat steamed idli or crisp dosa with coconut chutney. In Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, poha, flattened rice cooked with onion, peanuts and turmeric, is everywhere. Indore is famous for poha topped with sev and a squeeze of lemon.

Punjabi families often eat parathas stuffed with potato, with curd and pickle. Kerala has puttu, steamed rice flour layered with coconut, and Bengal has fluffy fried luchi. In the north-east, many families eat rice for breakfast, while Gujarati homes might serve thepla, a soft spiced flatbread that also travels well on long train journeys. A full tour of [[@indian-breakfasts|Indian breakfasts]] would take weeks of eating, and every region argues that its own is best.

In Turkey, breakfast is called kahvaltı, meaning "before [[@coffee|coffee]]". It's often a table full of small plates: cheese, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, eggs, honey and bread. In Nigeria, children may eat akara, fried bean fritters, with a smooth corn porridge called pap.

In [[@mexico|Mexico]], chilaquiles are fried tortilla pieces simmered in red or green salsa, often with eggs. In Brazil, children love pão de queijo, small cheese breads. In France, many children dunk bread or croissants in a bowl of hot chocolate. In Britain, a "full English" with eggs, beans, toast and sausages is a weekend favourite.

In the 1890s, John Harvey Kellogg ran a health resort in Battle Creek, Michigan. He and his brother Will Keith Kellogg made flakes of wheat and then corn as a plain food for patients. Will added sugar, started a company and sold [[@cereal-history|cereal]] to the whole country.

Cereal grew popular because it's quick: no cooking, just pour milk. Bright boxes, cartoon mascots and free toys inside helped sell it to children from the 1950s on. Today it's eaten worldwide, though many brands are high in sugar.

Many children have no breakfast at home, often because families are busy or short of money. Some schools step in. The United States made its School Breakfast Program permanent in 1975, and millions of students eat a free or cheap breakfast at school each day.

In 2022 Tamil Nadu began serving a free hot breakfast, such as upma or khichdi, to young children in government schools. It adds to India's [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]], the lunch served to crores of schoolchildren. text: Nobody knows exactly who wore the first shoes, because early shoes were made of bark, grass and animal skin, which rot away. But we have clues.

The oldest shoes ever found are woven sandals from Fort Rock Cave in Oregon, in the United States, made about 9,000 to 10,000 years ago. Scientists think people were wearing some kind of footwear much earlier, perhaps 40,000 years ago, based on changes in their toe bones. The first shoes were probably simple wraps of hide tied around the foot, to protect it from cold, sharp stones and thorns.

sec.t:
Walking barefoot makes the small bones in your toes strong and thick. Wearing shoes takes some of that load away, so over time, the toes of people who wear shoes become slightly thinner.

The American anthropologist Erik Trinkaus compared toe bones from [[@human-evolution|early humans]]. He found that toes began getting thinner around 40,000 years ago, during the last [[@ice-ages|ice age]]. His idea is that people had started wrapping their feet. Not every scientist agrees on the exact date, but it is a clever way to find a shoe without finding a shoe.

In 1991 hikers in the [[@switzerland|Alps]] found the body of a man who had died about 5,300 years ago. Scientists call him Ötzi. His shoes had soles of bearskin, tops of deerskin and a net of string stuffed with dry grass to keep his feet warm.

In 2010 an even older leather shoe turned up in a cave in Armenia. It was about 5,500 years old, made from one piece of cowhide laced around the foot, and it was stuffed with grass too.

In India, wooden sandals called paduka or khadau have been worn for a very long time. They have a knob that sits between the big toe and the next one. In the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], Bharata places Rama's padukas on the throne while Rama is in exile. Leather shoes such as the jutti of Punjab and the Kolhapuri chappal of Maharashtra are still made by hand today.

For long stretches of history, many shoes were made on straight wooden forms, so either shoe fitted either foot. Shaped left and right shoes became normal in Europe and America only during the 1800s, when new machines made them cheaper to produce.

In 1839 the American inventor Charles Goodyear found a way to toughen rubber with heat and sulphur. Rubber soles soon followed. By the early 1900s, canvas shoes with rubber soles were sold for sports, the ancestors of today's [[@sneakers|sneakers]]. Shoes have changed a great deal since the Fort Rock sandals, but the job is the same: keeping feet safe from the ground.

text: Some new [[species|species]] are not hiding in unexplored jungles. They have been seen many times, but everyone thought they were the same as a known animal.

sec.t:
On 4 November 2026, researchers led by the University of Salford in the UK announced two new species of howler monkey from South America. They are called Alouatta iroi, from the Guianas, and Alouatta matogrossensis, the Mato Grosso red howler, from southern Amazonia in Brazil. Live Science reported the discovery on 13 November.

The team studied the genomes, the complete DNA instructions, of 11 kinds of howler monkey, and matched them with measurements of museum specimens. Animals that had been lumped together as one species turned out to belong to separate family lines.

The [[@brazil-amazon|Amazon]] is crossed by giant rivers such as the Amazon itself, the Rio Branco and the Xingu. Howler monkeys spend almost their whole lives high in the forest [[canopy|canopy]]. To them, a wide river is like a wall.

When a group of animals is cut off for a very long time, it slowly changes in its own way. The study found that these rivers have kept howler populations apart for millions of years, helping new species form. This is one reason [[@rainforests|rainforests]] are bursting with so many kinds of life.

Howler monkeys live in Central and South America. They eat mostly leaves and use their strong tail like a fifth hand to hold on to branches. At dawn, males roar to tell other groups where they are. A special hollow bone in the throat makes the sound boom, and it can carry several kilometres through the trees, which puts howlers among the [[@extreme-loudest-animals|loudest animals]] on land.

Southern Amazonia is one of the fastest-changing landscapes on Earth, as forest is cleared for farms. The scientists warn that the new species may already be at risk because their [[habitat|habitat]] is shrinking. Naming them is the first step: an animal must be known before it can be counted and protected.
